title: Airport runway design: orientation, crosswind and length corrections
examples: How do you calculate the crosswind component?
Why do high airports need longer runways?

stages.label: Height: 2280 m
stages.ask: How is runway length corrected for elevation and temperature?

explain.say: Daocheng Yading airport in China sits about four thousand four hundred metres above sea level, and its runway is about four point two kilometres long. Thin, warm air gives wings less lift and engines less push, so planes need a longer run. Watch how a basic runway length grows with height, heat and slope.

draw.text: Airport runway design: orientation, crosswind and length corrections

stages.label: Height: 2280 m
stages.ask: How is runway length corrected for elevation and temperature?

explain.say: Each correction adds a share. Seven percent for every three hundred metres of height: six hundred metres adds fourteen percent, giving two thousand two hundred and eighty metres. Then one percent per degree hotter than standard air, and ten percent per one percent of slope. The two thousand metre runway grows to almost two thousand eight hundred.

stages.label: Height: 2280 m
stages.ask: How is runway length corrected for elevation and temperature?

explain.say: Now direction. Planes take off and land into the wind, and dislike wind from the side. The side push is the crosswind: wind speed times the sine of the angle to the runway. Look at the curve: a twenty knot wind at thirty degrees gives ten knots of crosswind. At ninety degrees, the full twenty.

explain.say: For a medium runway the crosswind limit is thirteen knots. See where the curve crosses the limit line: about forty degrees. So engineers study years of wind records, the wind rose, and point the runway so it can be used at least ninety five percent of the time. Its number is its magnetic heading over ten: runway nine faces east.

explain.say: Runway pavements are thick, because big jets press their tyres down hard, and grooved, so water drains away. Brilliant! Exam tip: apply height, then temperature, then slope, in that order. Challenge: a runway points two hundred and fifty degrees magnetic. What numbers are painted at each end?

layers.label: Asphalt or concrete
layers.note: Thick: big jet tyres press about 1.5 MPa
layers.ask: Why are runway pavements so thick?

faq.a: By their magnetic heading divided by ten and rounded. A runway facing 090 degrees is runway 09, and the same strip used the other way, facing 270 degrees, is runway 27.

faq.q: How do you calculate the crosswind component?
faq.a: Multiply the wind speed by the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway. A 20 knot wind at 30 degrees gives 10 knots of crosswind.

faq.q: What is the allowable crosswind for a runway?
faq.a: ICAO uses 20 knots for runways 1,500 metres or longer, 13 knots for 1,200 to 1,500 metres and 10 knots for shorter ones. The runway should be usable at least 95 percent of the time.

faq.q: How is runway length corrected for elevation and temperature?
faq.a: The basic length is raised 7 percent per 300 metres of elevation, then 1 percent per degree Celsius by which the reference temperature exceeds the standard atmosphere temperature at that height, then for gradient.
asks: Why do high airports need longer runways?

faq.q: Why are runway pavements so thick?
faq.a: Large aircraft put very heavy loads on a few wheels with high tyre pressures, often around 1.5 megapascals, so the pavement must spread those loads safely to the soil, for decades.

facts: ICAO corrects basic runway length by 7% per 300 m of elevation and 1% per °C above the standard atmosphere temperature.
ICAO recommends that a runway system be usable at least 95% of the time, judged from wind records.
